Infinite tensor products and their reference states

Written by GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI), Ultra, September–October 2026. Public domain (CC0).

Finite tensor products combine algebras. An infinite tensor product also needs a rule for embedding each finite part into the next. Units supply that rule for C*-algebras. Unit vectors supply it for Hilbert spaces. Normal reference states then determine the von Neumann algebra obtained in the product state's GNS representation.

We assume finite minimal C*-tensor products, GNS representations, Kaplansky density in the strong* topology, concrete preduals and the spectral theorem. The full finite von Neumann commutation theorem and normal slice maps used in Sections 2, 4 and 5 are proved in Spatial tensor commutants and arbitrary product-state supports, Sections 1–6. Its whole spectral-band graph construction and normal amplification/corner transfer retain arbitrary Hilbert spaces and arbitrary representations. Its Sections 7–8 give arbitrary-index product-state supports and the different central GNS kernel, including nonfaithful states. Section 16 below spells out the applications and the full general product modular graph. The inductive-limit construction can also be compared with AF-algebras, Section 4.

The universal normal-limit comparison in Proposition 2.1 uses the canonical C*-bidual, its predual A∗A^*A∗, the unique normal extension of a *-homomorphism into a von Neumann algebra, and the surjectivity of that extension onto the represented algebra. These are exactly Sections 3–8 of OA-MOD's Every bounded functional becomes normal in one representation, already used in Nuclear biduals and extensions. It also uses the C*-quotient norm and the trace-class description of a concrete von Neumann predual.

For the modular part we use the closed Tomita involution S=JΔ1/2S=J\Delta^{1/2}S=JΔ1/2, JMJ=M′JMJ=M'JMJ=M′, and modular implementation from The modular fundamental theorem. Normality of a normal state's GNS representation is WG-007 in General weights: finite domains, GNS spaces, and normal representations. The final criterion uses exactly the separable-predual theorem of Pointwise inner flows and continuous implementers: a continuous real action whose individual automorphisms are inner has a continuous implementing unitary group. It also uses TI-06 in Trace densities and noncommutative integration and CZ-05, 08 and 11 in Fixed elements and changes of density. These are modular and flow prerequisites, not proofs supplied by this lesson.

Inner products are linear in the second variable. All index sets and Hilbert spaces in Sections 2–6 may be arbitrary. Sections 7–8 concern sequences; Section 8 additionally assumes separable preduals. Further reading is listed at the end.

Begin with a finite observation

An infinite product can be studied through three questions: which reference sector is being used, what its finite-coordinate observations retain, and whether the local data determine a global operator or unitary. The first calculation shows why recovery and multiplication are different questions.

Take two copies of C2\mathbb C^2C2, use e1e_1e1​ as the second reference vector, and let Vη=η⊗e1V\eta=\eta\otimes e_1Vη=η⊗e1​. For the unit vector

b=(e1⊗e1+e2⊗e2)/2,b=(e_1\otimes e_1+e_2\otimes e_2)/\sqrt2,b=(e1​⊗e1​+e2​⊗e2​)/2​,

write PbP_bPb​ for its rank-one projection. Then V∗b=e1/2V^*b=e_1/\sqrt2V∗b=e1​/2​, so the finite observation is

(V∗PbV)⊗1=12Pe1⊗1.(V^*P_bV)\otimes1=\tfrac12P_{e_1}\otimes1.(V∗Pb​V)⊗1=21​Pe1​​⊗1.

This is positive and its square is half itself. Thus a projection need not remain a projection under a reference-vector observation. The original operator is recovered by allowing the retained coordinates to grow, as Theorem 4.1 proves; multiplicativity of each observation is not required. Exercise 5 develops this calculation in full.

The route through the constructions is:

  • Choose the reference sector, then construct its finite observations and test the state, factor and trace.
  • Track phase as well as overlap before assembling local implementing unitaries.
  • Read the modular flow and the semifiniteness test from the chosen states and their support corners.
  • Use the separate stage-map construction to handle algebraic identifications, loss of norm and kernels. It proves the completion and universal property used for the abstract product algebra.

The Hilbert-space reference sector and the universal normal limit answer different questions. The binary-state example in Proposition 2.1 makes that distinction explicit. The final stage-map construction also explains why an algebraic germ can survive while its limiting norm vanishes.

Proposition 2.1. Let A=⨂j=1∞M2A=\bigotimes_{j=1}^\infty M_2A=⨂j=1∞​M2​, with local algebras An=M2nA_n=M_{2^n}An​=M2n​. Every reference-state product representation of these countably many matrix algebras, however, generates a von Neumann algebra with separable predual.

Proof. Each canonical inclusion An→A∗∗A_n\to A^{**}An​→A∗∗ is normal, since AnA_nAn​ is finite-dimensional. The canonical bidual extension theorem gives a unique normal unital extension A∗∗→NA^{**}\to NA∗∗→N. Uniqueness follows from the ultraweak density of AAA in A∗∗A^{**}A∗∗. This is the claimed universal property.

For each binary sequence s=(sj)∈{0,1}Ns=(s_j)\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}s=(sj​)∈{0,1}N, take the product of the one-mode vector states at the basis vectors labelled sjs_jsj​, obtaining a state ψs\psi_sψs​ on AAA. Positivity and existence are the product GNS construction above. Write eje_jej​ for the occupation projection in coordinate jjj. If s≠ts\ne ts=t, choose jjj with sj≠tjs_j\ne t_jsj​=tj​. ∥ψs−ψt∥=2.(6a)\|\psi_s-\psi_t\|=2. \tag{6a}∥ψs​−ψt​∥=2.(6a)

The upper bound is the triangle inequality for two states, and the unitary proves the lower bound. Thus A∗A^*A∗, the canonical predual of A∗∗A^{**}A∗∗, contains an uncountable set with pairwise distance two. A separable metric space cannot contain such a set: balls of radius less than one about its elements are disjoint and must each contain a different point of a countable dense set. Hence this predual is nonseparable.

For any one-mode normal reference states, their GNS spaces have dimension at most four. The countable pointed tensor product therefore has a countable dense set of local vectors and is separable. A von Neumann algebra represented on this space has predual a quotient of its separable coefficient completion, as proved above, hence separable. It consequently cannot be the universal algebra A∗∗A^{**}A∗∗ above. The normal extension of the GNS representation is onto this generated algebra, by the full normal-extension image proof above. Specifying reference states therefore chooses a normal quotient of the universal bidual, with its particular GNS realization; it does not merely rename the universal normal inductive limit. □\square□

8. Test semifiniteness on the support corner

A normal state can have a proper support even in its faithful factor representation. We first identify its full support corner, retain the separable-predual hypothesis there, and construct the traces needed to return from that corner to the original factor. The general semifiniteness proofs supply the countability, trace-density, trace-transfer and continuous-implementation arguments used below. In the density formula, products with an unbounded density mean the actual trace-integrable pairing constructed there.

ωn(x)=τn(hnx),\omega_n(x)=\tau_n(h_nx),ωn​(x)=τn​(hn​x),

one has

∑n=1∞(1−∣ωn(hnit)∣)<∞for every t∈R.(21)\sum_{n=1}^\infty\left(1-|\omega_n(h_n^{it})|\right)<\infty \qquad\hbox{for every }t\in\mathbb R. \tag{21}n=1∑∞​(1−∣ωn​(hnit​)∣)<∞for every t∈R.(21)

Here hnith_n^{it}hnit​ is a unitary on s(hn)s(h_n)s(hn​), and is defined to be zero on its orthogonal complement when evaluated in the displayed state.

Proof. Put pn=s(ωn)p_n=s(\omega_n)pn​=s(ωn​), and use the normal GNS representation of each state. This representation is faithful: its kernel is the central ideal complementary to the central carrier of pnp_npn​, and a nonzero state on a factor has central carrier one. The state itself need not be faithful. By the full support-corner construction,

e=sM(ω)=s-lim⁡N→∞(p1⊗⋯⊗pN⊗1),eΩ=Ω≠0,e=s_M(\omega)=\operatorname*{s-lim}_{N\to\infty} (p_1\otimes\cdots\otimes p_N\otimes1),\qquad e\Omega=\Omega\ne0,e=sM​(ω)=N→∞s-lim​(p1​⊗⋯⊗pN​⊗1),eΩ=Ω=0,

and the actual compression on its full range is the normal isomorphism

eMe≅⨂n(pnMnpn,ωn∣pnMnpn).(22) eMe\cong\bigotimes_n(p_nM_np_n,\omega_n|_{p_nM_np_n}). \tag{22}eMe≅n⨂​(pn​Mn​pn​,ωn​∣pn​Mn​pn​​).(22)

Normal compression of the ultraweakly dense local union proves the onto algebra equality. The restricted states are faithful, the corners are nonzero factors, and their preduals are separable. The countability construction also makes the whole corner product predual separable: countably many bounded ultraweak tests give total GNS vectors, countably many finite excitations give a separable pointed Hilbert completion, and the coefficient completion and its concrete-predual quotient stay separable.

The matrix-trace transport proves that any specified nonzero corner of a factor has an NSF trace exactly when the factor does. It restricts traces in one direction. In the other, a maximal family of partial isometries identifies the factor with a corner of an arbitrary matrix amplification of the given corner; its positive diagonal sum constructs an NSF trace and transports it back. Thus this equivalence applies to every pnMnpnp_nM_np_npn​Mn​pn​ and to eMeeMeeMe. No type-classification inference is needed for the existence of these traces.

We next establish the precise modular test. For a von Neumann algebra PPP with separable predual and faithful normal state φ\varphiφ, an NSF trace τ\tauτ has a unique positive trace-integrable state density hhh, with support one. The whole trace-density and perturbation argument gives

φ(x)=τ(hx),σtφ(x)=hitxh−it. \varphi(x)=\tau(hx),\qquad \sigma_t^\varphi(x)=h^{it}xh^{-it}.φ(x)=τ(hx),σtφ​(x)=hitxh−it.

σtτ=Ad⁡(k−it)∘σtφ=id⁡.(20) \sigma_t^\tau =\operatorname{Ad}(k^{-it})\circ\sigma_t^\varphi =\operatorname{id}. \tag{20}σtτ​=Ad(k−it)∘σtφ​=id.(20)

Apply it to the faithful states in (22). Their product modular flow is the product of their component modular flows, by Theorem 6.1 and the complete graph in Section 16.3. For each fixed real ttt, Theorem 7.2 detects innerness of that product flow by component innerness and its exact overlap series.

Suppose first that MMM is semifinite. The corner eMeeMeeMe is semifinite, so its modular time maps are inner. Theorem 7.2 makes every component modular time map inner. Its separable predual permits the continuous-implementation construction, and (20) constructs an NSF trace there. Matrix-trace transport extends an NSF trace to MMM. Both implications hold for the original arbitrary normal states. □\square□

The general factor-trace uniqueness proof compares rational diagonal projections, finds a common finite cut for two arbitrary NSF traces, and passes through normal finite sandwiches. It proves that every NSF trace on a nonzero factor is a positive scalar multiple of any other. If τn\tau_nτn​ is replaced by anτna_n\tau_nan​τn​, uniqueness of the density gives an−1hna_n^{-1}h_nan−1​hn​. Separate spectral calculus on pnHnp_nH_npn​Hn​ therefore gives

Both powers are zero off pnp_npn​ when evaluated in the state. Their moduli agree, so the defect series is intrinsic to the states. The argument tests each real time separately; it asserts no uniformity in time. The arbitrary-index commutant theorem supplies no replacement for the sequence and separable-predual hypotheses of this criterion.

1. Construct the algebra from its stage maps

The norm of a stage element can decrease as it moves through the system. We first impose the algebraic stage relations, quotient by elements of limiting norm zero, and complete. F01–F10 establish the C*-norm and quotient facts used below. F11 constructs the limit for arbitrary directed indices; F12 gives its maps and kernels; F14 proves the extension condition for general normed systems.

∥S(en(a))∥=∥ψm(ϕm,n(a))∥≤∥ϕm,n(a)∥.\|S(e_n(a))\|=\|\psi_m(\phi_{m,n}(a))\| \le\|\phi_{m,n}(a)\|.∥S(en​(a))∥=∥ψm​(ϕm,n​(a))∥≤∥ϕm,n​(a)∥.

It preserves products and adjoints because these operations are continuous and it preserves them on the dense subalgebra E/NE/NE/N. The extension is unique: every *-homomorphism between C*-algebras is continuous by F05, and its values on the dense union are prescribed.

If the connecting maps are injective, F07 makes their composites isometric. The infimum defining p(en(a))p(e_n(a))p(en​(a)) then equals ∥a∥\|a\|∥a∥, so each ιn\iota_nιn​ is isometric. This construction works even when the algebraic limit has nonclosed kernels. For example, let An=C0([n,∞))A_n=C_0([n,\infty))An​=C0​([n,∞)), with restriction as connecting map. The algebraic limit consists of germs at infinity. The germ of e−te^{-t}e−t is nonzero, but every germ has p=0p=0p=0, because

sup⁡t≥m∣a(t)∣⟶0.\sup_{t\ge m}|a(t)|\longrightarrow0.t≥msup​∣a(t)∣⟶0.

The C*-limit is therefore zero. Any *-representation of the algebraic limit is zero: its restriction to each AnA_nAn​ is contractive, so the same estimate forces every represented germ to vanish. A closed eventual kernel, the source's “properness” condition, allows completion without this additional null quotient. It is not necessary for existence of the C*-limit.

FI04 proves the stage and restriction-map assertions and the nonzero exponential germ. F12 gives the arbitrary directed and cofinal kernel formulas.

Proof. A C*-homomorphism induces an isometric injection of its quotient by the kernel into its target. Therefore

∥ϕm,n(a)∥=dist⁡(a,Kn,m).\|\phi_{m,n}(a)\|=\operatorname{dist}(a,K_{n,m}).∥ϕm,n​(a)∥=dist(a,Kn,m​).

The kernels increase with mmm. Taking the infimum of these distances gives the distance to their union, proving (1a). For a sufficiently late stage with closed KnK_nKn​, zero distance means a∈Kna\in K_na∈Kn​. Some later image of aaa is then zero, so [a]=0[a]=0[a]=0 in the algebraic limit. Every algebraic class has a representative at such a late stage. Hence ppp is faithful on the whole algebraic limit. The completion in Theorem 1.1 then needs no further null quotient. This is precisely what the source's properness hypothesis supplies. If KnK_nKn​ is not closed, an element of Kn‾∖Kn\overline{K_n}\setminus K_nKn​​∖Kn​ instead gives a nonzero algebraic class of seminorm zero. □\square□

F10 proves the kernel-distance identity, F12 proves cofinal closedness suffices, and F15 proves the following AF consequence.

An AF-algebra here means a C*-limit of a sequence of finite-dimensional C*-algebras. Equivalently it has an increasing sequence of finite-dimensional subalgebras with norm-dense union: the images in Theorem 1.1 are finite-dimensional and hence closed. Such an algebra is separable, by taking rational complex combinations of bases at each stage. Approximation by a directed family on an arbitrary index set is a different countability convention and should be stated separately.

Exercise 1. Let An=C3A_n=\mathbb C^3An​=C3, with ϕn(a,b,c)=(a,c,c)\phi_n(a,b,c)=(a,c,c)ϕn​(a,b,c)=(a,c,c) at every stage. Determine the C*-limit and its canonical maps.

∥ιn(a,b,c)∥=max⁡(∣a∣,∣c∣).\|\iota_n(a,b,c)\|=\max(|a|,|c|).∥ιn​(a,b,c)∥=max(∣a∣,∣c∣).

∥fi−fj∥≥∣(fi−fj)(Zi)∣=1.\|f_i-f_j\|\ge |(f_i-f_j)(Z_i)|=1.∥fi​−fj​∥≥∣(fi​−fj​)(Zi​)∣=1.

The separated-ball argument now proves that the predual is nonseparable. By Corollary 5.3 the product is nevertheless a finite factor: its faithful normalized product trace and factorality hold for this uncountable index set. Neither property forces separability.

Exercise 8. Let Mn=M2M_n=M_2Mn​=M2​ and ωn(x)=Tr⁡(diag⁡(pn,1−pn)x)\omega_n(x)=\operatorname{Tr}(\operatorname{diag}(p_n,1-p_n)x)ωn​(x)=Tr(diag(pn​,1−pn​)x), where 0<pn<10<p_n<10<pn​<1. Express the summand of (21) using pnp_npn​ and ttt.

Solution. With the ordinary matrix trace, the density is hn=diag⁡(pn,1−pn)h_n=\operatorname{diag}(p_n,1-p_n)hn​=diag(pn​,1−pn​). Both entries are positive, so

ωn(hnit)=pn pnit+(1−pn)(1−pn)it.\omega_n(h_n^{it}) =p_n\,p_n^{it}+(1-p_n)(1-p_n)^{it}.ωn​(hnit​)=pn​pnit​+(1−pn​)(1−pn​)it.

1−∣pn 1+it+(1−pn) 1+it∣.1-\left|p_n^{\,1+it}+(1-p_n)^{\,1+it}\right|.1−​pn1+it​+(1−pn​)1+it​.

For a completely real form, set q=pnq=p_nq=pn​ and ϑ=tlog⁡(q/(1−q))\vartheta=t\log(q/(1-q))ϑ=tlog(q/(1−q)). Expanding the modulus square gives

1−4pn(1−pn)sin⁡2 ⁣(t2log⁡pn1−pn).1-4p_n(1-p_n)\sin^2\!\left(\frac t2\log\frac{p_n}{1-p_n}\right).1−4pn​(1−pn​)sin2(2t​log1−pn​pn​​).

If the normalized trace is used instead, the density is 2hn2h_n2hn​, which multiplies the displayed state value by 2it2^{it}2it; its modulus, and hence the summand, is unchanged.

For a constant p≠1/2p\ne1/2p=1/2, take t=π/log⁡(p/(1−p))t=\pi/\log(p/(1-p))t=π/log(p/(1−p)). The summand becomes

at every coordinate, so its sum diverges. Exercise 9. Suppose ωn\omega_nωn​ is a pure vector state on B(Kn)B(K_n)B(Kn​), with Kn≠0K_n\ne0Kn​=0 arbitrary. Identify the product von Neumann algebra and reconcile it with (21) in the separable case.

Solution. Choose the unit vector ξn\xi_nξn​ defining ωn\omega_nωn​. The one-leg GNS map [x]↦xξn[x]\mapsto x\xi_n[x]↦xξn​ is isometric because its squared norm is ωn(x∗x)\omega_n(x^*x)ωn​(x∗x), and is onto KnK_nKn​: the rank-one operator z↦η⟨ξn,z⟩z\mapsto\eta\langle\xi_n,z\ranglez↦η⟨ξn​,z⟩ sends ξn\xi_nξn​ to any η∈Kn\eta\in K_nη∈Kn​. The GNS representation under this map is the identity representation of B(Kn)B(K_n)B(Kn​), hence faithful and normal. When dim⁡Kn>1\dim K_n>1dimKn​>1, its vector state is still nonfaithful. Thus the product GNS space is

H=⨂n(Kn,ξn),H=\bigotimes_n(K_n,\xi_n),H=n⨂​(Kn​,ξn​),

with the local full-operator actions.

These actions generate B(H)B(H)B(H). For a finite FFF, elementary tensor rank-one operators lie in the local algebra and span rank-one operators on a dense tensor-vector space; their norm limits give all rank-one operators on HFH_FHF​. Hence their commutant on HFH_FHF​ is scalar. If xxx commutes with all local actions, bimodularity makes EF(x)∈B(HF)⊗1E_F(x)\in B(H_F)\otimes1EF​(x)∈B(HF​)⊗1 commute with that finite full-operator action, so EF(x)=cF1E_F(x)=c_F1EF​(x)=cF​1. State preservation makes cF=⟨Ω,xΩ⟩c_F=\langle\Omega,x\Omega\ranglecF​=⟨Ω,xΩ⟩ independent of FFF. Since EF(x)→xE_F(x)\to xEF​(x)→x strongly, xxx is scalar. Taking the commutant again proves M=B(H)M=B(H)M=B(H), a type I, semifinite factor, without requiring any KnK_nKn​ to be separable.

In the separable setting of (21), use the usual operator trace and density hn=Pξnh_n=P_{\xi_n}hn​=Pξn​​. Its imaginary power is the identity on its one-dimensional support and zero on the complement, exactly as specified in that formula. Therefore ωn(hnit)=1\omega_n(h_n^{it})=1ωn​(hnit​)=1 and every summand is zero. This agrees with M=B(H)M=B(H)M=B(H); it does not require the pure reference state to be faithful on the full operator algebra.

Exercise 10. Why can the conditional expectations EFE_FEF​ have a fixed state without that state being faithful? Give a finite example and state the correct faithfulness condition for the product GNS model.

Solution. In (10), VFΩF=ΩV_F\Omega_F=\OmegaVF​ΩF​=Ω, so compression followed by amplification gives

⟨Ω,EF(x)Ω⟩=⟨ΩF,VF∗xVFΩF⟩=⟨Ω,xΩ⟩.\langle\Omega,E_F(x)\Omega\rangle =\langle\Omega_F,V_F^*xV_F\Omega_F\rangle =\langle\Omega,x\Omega\rangle.⟨Ω,EF​(x)Ω⟩=⟨ΩF​,VF∗​xVF​ΩF​⟩=⟨Ω,xΩ⟩.

This equality uses the reference vector, not faithfulness. For instance, on B(C2)B(\mathbb C^2)B(C2), with Ω=e1\Omega=e_1Ω=e1​, the scalar expectation E∅(x)=⟨e1,xe1⟩1E_\varnothing(x)=\langle e_1,xe_1\rangle1E∅​(x)=⟨e1​,xe1​⟩1 fixes the vector state but kills the nonzero projection Pe2P_{e_2}Pe2​​.

The exact condition in the product GNS representation is that every ξi\xi_iξi​ be separating for the represented component πi(Mi)\pi_i(M_i)πi​(Mi​). Necessity follows by padding a nonzero component operator aia_iai​ with aiξi=0a_i\xi_i=0ai​ξi​=0: it is still nonzero and kills Ω\OmegaΩ. For sufficiency, separation makes ξi\xi_iξi​ cyclic for the component commutant: the projection onto πi(Mi)′ξi‾\overline{\pi_i(M_i)'\xi_i}πi​(Mi​)′ξi​​ belongs to πi(Mi)\pi_i(M_i)πi​(Mi​), fixes ξi\xi_iξi​, and must be one. Finite products of these commutant orbits are dense in the pointed Hilbert space. Every product operator commutes with them, so an operator killing Ω\OmegaΩ kills a dense set and is zero. Thus Ω\OmegaΩ is separating, equivalently its vector state is faithful.

For normal states on factors, the component GNS representations are faithful, and this condition is exactly faithfulness of every ωi\omega_iωi​. For general algebras it concerns their represented, state-supported central quotients: evaluation at the first coordinate of C2\mathbb C^2C2 is not faithful on C2\mathbb C^2C2, but its one-dimensional GNS image carries a faithful state. Faithfulness of a GNS representation and faithfulness of its reference state are distinct assertions. Normality alone does not settle the separating-vector condition: the finite vector state above is normal and nonfaithful.

Exercise 11. Derive (1a), and apply it to the germ example in Section 1. Why does the class of e−te^{-t}e−t survive algebraically but disappear in the C*-limit?

Solution. Fix a stage nnn. For m≥nm\ge nm≥n, the induced map

An/ker⁡ϕm,n⟶Am,a+ker⁡ϕm,n⟼ϕm,n(a)A_n/\ker\phi_{m,n}\longrightarrow A_m,\qquad a+\ker\phi_{m,n}\longmapsto\phi_{m,n}(a)An​/kerϕm,n​⟶Am​,a+kerϕm,n​⟼ϕm,n​(a)

is an injective C*-homomorphism. The quotient-norm and isometry proofs F10 and F07 therefore give

∥ϕm,n(a)∥=dist⁡(a,Kn,m).\|\phi_{m,n}(a)\|=\operatorname{dist}(a,K_{n,m}).∥ϕm,n​(a)∥=dist(a,Kn,m​).

The kernels Kn,mK_{n,m}Kn,m​ increase with mmm. Taking the infimum is the same as allowing every element of their union, so

p([a])=inf⁡m≥ndist⁡(a,Kn,m)=dist⁡ ⁣(a,⋃m≥nKn,m)=dist⁡(a,Kn),p([a])=\inf_{m\ge n}\operatorname{dist}(a,K_{n,m}) =\operatorname{dist}\!\left(a,\bigcup_{m\ge n}K_{n,m}\right) =\operatorname{dist}(a,K_n),p([a])=m≥ninf​dist(a,Kn,m​)=dist(a,m≥n⋃​Kn,m​)=dist(a,Kn​),

which is (1a). No nearest point or attainment of an infimum is required.

For the restriction system C0([n,∞))C_0([n,\infty))C0​([n,∞)), KnK_nKn​ consists of functions identically zero beyond some finite point. It is dense: the continuous cutoff χR\chi_RχR​, equal to one up to RRR, linear down to zero on [R,R+1][R,R+1][R,R+1], and zero afterward, satisfies

χRf∈Kn,∥f−χRf∥∞≤sup⁡t≥R∣f(t)∣⟶0.\chi_Rf\in K_n,\qquad \|f-\chi_Rf\|_\infty\le\sup_{t\ge R}|f(t)|\longrightarrow0.χR​f∈Kn​,∥f−χR​f∥∞​≤t≥Rsup​∣f(t)∣⟶0.

But e−t∉Kne^{-t}\notin K_ne−t∈/Kn​, since it is strictly positive at every point of every tail. Thus the dense eventual kernel KnK_nKn​ is not closed, and its algebraic germ is nonzero. Its later norms are exactly

∥e−t∣[m,∞)∥∞=e−m⟶0,\|e^{-t}|_{[m,\infty)}\|_\infty=e^{-m}\longrightarrow0,∥e−t∣[m,∞)​∥∞​=e−m⟶0,

so (1a) makes its limiting seminorm zero. In fact the same tail estimate makes p=0p=0p=0 for every germ, and the completed C*-limit is the zero algebra. Algebraic equality requires eventual exact vanishing; the additional null quotient also removes arbitrarily small tails. When eventual kernels are closed at all sufficiently late stages, (1a) shows that every zero-seminorm element represented there actually belongs to KnK_nKn​, and so becomes exactly zero at a later stage. Passing any earlier element to such a stage gives the same conclusion. Closed eventual kernels therefore remove this additional algebraic-versus-norm defect.

Exercise 12. Why are all the binary product states in Proposition 2.1 normal on A∗∗A^{**}A∗∗, but they cannot all extend normally to one reference-state product algebra?

Solution. Construct a binary state ψs\psi_sψs​, for s∈{0,1}Ns\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}s∈{0,1}N, from its finite vectors es1⊗⋯⊗esNe_{s_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{s_N}es1​​⊗⋯⊗esN​​. Their vector functionals agree under unit padding and have norm one, so they extend to a state on A=⨂nM2A=\bigotimes_nM_2A=⨂n​M2​. Such a state is an element of A∗A^*A∗. In the canonical bidual with predual A∗A^*A∗, its extension is

ψ~s(X)=X(ψs)(X∈A∗∗).\widetilde\psi_s(X)=X(\psi_s)\qquad(X\in A^{**}).ψ​s​(X)=X(ψs​)(X∈A∗∗).

It is weak* continuous by this defining evaluation, and is the normal positive state extension furnished by the bidual construction. Thus all binary states are normal there; this is one reason the universal normal algebra is larger than a single reference-state realization.

A normal extension to one reference-product algebra MMM, if it exists, is unique: the local image of AAA is ultraweakly dense, and normal functionals agreeing there agree on all of MMM. Restriction to AAA is contractive on functionals. Suppose all binary states had such extensions. If s≠ts\ne ts=t, choose a differing coordinate jjj, and let eje_jej​ be its occupation projection. The local selfadjoint unitary 2ej−12e_j-12ej​−1 has opposite values, so the extensions satisfy

∥ψ~s−ψ~t∥≥∣(ψ~s−ψ~t)(2ej−1)∣=2.\|\widetilde\psi_s-\widetilde\psi_t\| \ge|(\widetilde\psi_s-\widetilde\psi_t)(2e_j-1)|=2.∥ψ​s​−ψ​t​∥≥∣(ψ​s​−ψ​t​)(2ej​−1)∣=2.

The reverse bound is two because both are states. They would form an uncountable family at pairwise distance two in M∗M_*M∗​. But each one-mode GNS space has dimension at most four; a countable finite-support basis makes the reference-product Hilbert space separable. Its trace-class space is separable, and its quotient M∗M_*M∗​ is separable, by the concrete-predual calculation in Section 2. A separable normed space cannot contain that separated family. Hence the binary states cannot all extend normally to one reference product, although they all extend normally to A∗∗A^{**}A∗∗. Consequently a normal state extension to the universal bidual need not factor through the chosen normal quotient A∗∗→MA^{**}\to MA∗∗→M: factoring all of them would give precisely the impossible family of normal extensions just considered.

10. Hilbert and operator foundations for the finite-leg vector slice

The following argument supplies the direct foundations of the vector-compression proof preceding Lemma 7.1 in Infinite tensor products and their reference states. It works for arbitrary, possibly nonseparable complex Hilbert spaces and arbitrary concrete factors. It constructs the Hilbert tensor product, bounded mixed compressions, their concrete ultraweak normality, and the unital bicommutant step. It then gives the complete nonzero-intertwiner and scalar unitary normalization argument.

The foundation boundary is ZFC, real and complex scalar completeness, elementary algebra, and the definition of a Hilbert space as a complete complex inner-product space. A concrete von Neumann algebra means a unital selfadjoint subalgebra of B(H)B(H)B(H) closed in the weak operator topology. Its center is P∩P′P\cap P'P∩P′; a factor is nonzero and has center C1\mathbb C1C1. The concrete ultraweak topology is defined through countable Hilbert-space amplification below. Thus no trace-class duality, spectral theorem, abstract predual identification, normal representation existence theorem, general tensor commutation theorem, modular theorem, or infinite-product theorem is an input. If the word “factor” instead starts from an abstract algebra with a prescribed predual, this proof applies after faithful normal concrete realizations have been supplied; mere faithfulness does not supply that separate topology identification.

Throughout, the inner product is conjugate linear in its first argument and linear in its second. The Hilbert and concrete operator arguments below state the separate normal-realization inputs needed for abstract algebras.

10.1. Inner-product estimates and orthogonal projection

For vectors h,kh,kh,k with h≠0h\ne0h=0, expand the nonnegative quantity

∥k−⟨h,k⟩∥h∥2h∥2=∥k∥2−∣⟨h,k⟩∣2∥h∥2.\left\|k-\frac{\langle h,k\rangle}{\|h\|^2}h\right\|^2 =\|k\|^2-\frac{|\langle h,k\rangle|^2}{\|h\|^2}.​k−∥h∥2⟨h,k⟩​h​2=∥k∥2−∥h∥2∣⟨h,k⟩∣2​.

This proves ∣⟨h,k⟩∣≤∥h∥∥k∥|\langle h,k\rangle|\le\|h\|\|k\|∣⟨h,k⟩∣≤∥h∥∥k∥; the zero-vector case is immediate. Expansion also gives the parallelogram identity

∥h+k∥2+∥h−k∥2=2∥h∥2+2∥k∥2,\|h+k\|^2+\|h-k\|^2=2\|h\|^2+2\|k\|^2,∥h+k∥2+∥h−k∥2=2∥h∥2+2∥k∥2,

and Cauchy-Schwarz applied to the cross term gives the triangle inequality. In particular, inner products are continuous in each variable.

Let MMM be a closed linear subspace of a Hilbert space HHH, let x∈Hx\in Hx∈H, and put d=inf⁡m∈M∥x−m∥d=\inf_{m\in M}\|x-m\|d=infm∈M​∥x−m∥. Choose mn∈Mm_n\in Mmn​∈M with ∥x−mn∥2→d2\|x-m_n\|^2\to d^2∥x−mn​∥2→d2. The parallelogram identity and (mn+mj)/2∈M(m_n+m_j)/2\in M(mn​+mj​)/2∈M give

∥mn−mj∥2=2∥x−mn∥2+2∥x−mj∥2−4∥x−mn+mj2∥2≤2∥x−mn∥2+2∥x−mj∥2−4d2⟶0.\begin{aligned} \|m_n-m_j\|^2 &=2\|x-m_n\|^2+2\|x-m_j\|^2 -4\left\|x-\frac{m_n+m_j}{2}\right\|^2\\ &\le2\|x-m_n\|^2+2\|x-m_j\|^2-4d^2\longrightarrow0. \end{aligned}∥mn​−mj​∥2​=2∥x−mn​∥2+2∥x−mj​∥2−4​x−2mn​+mj​​​2≤2∥x−mn​∥2+2∥x−mj​∥2−4d2⟶0.​

Completeness and closedness give mn→m∈Mm_n\to m\in Mmn​→m∈M, and ∥x−m∥=d\|x-m\|=d∥x−m∥=d. Write r=x−mr=x-mr=x−m. For w∈Mw\in Mw∈M, minimality gives ∥r−tw∥2≥∥r∥2\|r-tw\|^2\ge\|r\|^2∥r−tw∥2≥∥r∥2 for every complex ttt. Expanding and first taking real ttt, then purely imaginary ttt, shows that both the real and imaginary parts of ⟨r,w⟩\langle r,w\rangle⟨r,w⟩ vanish. Thus r∈M⊥r\in M^\perpr∈M⊥.

The space M⊥M^\perpM⊥ is closed, being the intersection of the kernels of the continuous maps y↦⟨w,y⟩y\mapsto\langle w,y\rangley↦⟨w,y⟩, w∈Mw\in Mw∈M. Also M∩M⊥={0}M\cap M^\perp=\{0\}M∩M⊥={0}. We have proved the unique orthogonal decomposition x=m+rx=m+rx=m+r. Define pMx=mp_Mx=mpM​x=m. Uniqueness makes pMp_MpM​ linear, and Pythagoras gives ∥pMx∥≤∥x∥\|p_Mx\|\le\|x\|∥pM​x∥≤∥x∥. The decomposition shows pM2=pMp_M^2=p_MpM2​=pM​ and

⟨x,pMy⟩=⟨pMx,pMy⟩=⟨pMx,y⟩.\langle x,p_My\rangle=\langle p_Mx,p_My\rangle =\langle p_Mx,y\rangle.⟨x,pM​y⟩=⟨pM​x,pM​y⟩=⟨pM​x,y⟩.

Thus it is the bounded orthogonal projection onto MMM, of norm at most one. Its norm is one if M≠{0}M\ne\{0\}M={0}, while p{0}=0p_{\{0\}}=0p{0}​=0. No nonzero-subspace qualification is suppressed.

If a bounded operator aaa and its adjoint both preserve MMM, then aaa preserves M⊥M^\perpM⊥: for y∈M⊥y\in M^\perpy∈M⊥ and m∈Mm\in Mm∈M, ⟨m,ay⟩=⟨a∗m,y⟩=0\langle m,ay\rangle=\langle a^*m,y\rangle=0⟨m,ay⟩=⟨a∗m,y⟩=0. Applying aaa to the two parts of the decomposition therefore gives apM=pMaap_M=p_MaapM​=pM​a.

10.2. Riesz representation, adjoints and the operator C*-identity

Let f:H→Cf:H\to\mathbb Cf:H→C be a bounded linear functional. For f=0f=0f=0, the representing vector is zero. Otherwise choose yyy with f(y)=1f(y)=1f(y)=1, let M=ker⁡fM=\ker fM=kerf, and set z=y−pMyz=y-p_Myz=y−pM​y. Then z⊥Mz\perp Mz⊥M and f(z)=1f(z)=1f(z)=1, so z≠0z\ne0z=0. Since h−f(h)z∈Mh-f(h)z\in Mh−f(h)z∈M,

⟨z,h⟩=f(h)∥z∥2,f(h)=⟨z∥z∥2,h⟩.\langle z,h\rangle=f(h)\|z\|^2, \qquad f(h)=\left\langle\frac{z}{\|z\|^2},h\right\rangle.⟨z,h⟩=f(h)∥z∥2,f(h)=⟨∥z∥2z​,h⟩.

For a representing vector rrr, Cauchy-Schwarz gives ∥f∥≤∥r∥\|f\|\le\|r\|∥f∥≤∥r∥, and evaluation at r/∥r∥r/\|r\|r/∥r∥ gives equality when r≠0r\ne0r=0. If two vectors represent the same functional, evaluating their difference against itself proves equality. This proves the Hilbert Riesz theorem, with the anti-linear dependence of the representing vector on the functional.

For a bounded linear map T:H→LT:H\to LT:H→L and y∈Ly\in Ly∈L, apply this result to h↦⟨y,Th⟩h\mapsto\langle y,Th\rangleh↦⟨y,Th⟩. Its unique representing vector is denoted by T∗yT^*yT∗y, so

⟨T∗y,h⟩=⟨y,Th⟩,equivalently⟨h,T∗y⟩=⟨Th,y⟩.\langle T^*y,h\rangle=\langle y,Th\rangle, \quad\text{equivalently}\quad \langle h,T^*y\rangle=\langle Th,y\rangle.⟨T∗y,h⟩=⟨y,Th⟩,equivalently⟨h,T∗y⟩=⟨Th,y⟩.

Uniqueness and the inner-product scalar rules show that T∗T^*T∗ is linear. The functional estimate gives ∥T∗y∥≤∥T∥∥y∥\|T^*y\|\le\|T\|\|y\|∥T∗y∥≤∥T∥∥y∥, hence T∗T^*T∗ is bounded. For composable maps,

⟨(ST)∗y,h⟩=⟨y,STh⟩=⟨S∗y,Th⟩=⟨T∗S∗y,h⟩,\langle(ST)^*y,h\rangle =\langle y,STh\rangle =\langle S^*y,Th\rangle =\langle T^*S^*y,h\rangle,⟨(ST)∗y,h⟩=⟨y,STh⟩=⟨S∗y,Th⟩=⟨T∗S∗y,h⟩,

The operator norm obeys ∥ST∥≤∥S∥∥T∥\|ST\|\le\|S\|\|T\|∥ST∥≤∥S∥∥T∥. Moreover,

∥Th∥2=⟨h,T∗Th⟩≤∥T∗T∥∥h∥2,∥T∗T∥≤∥T∗∥∥T∥=∥T∥2.\|Th\|^2=\langle h,T^*Th\rangle \le\|T^*T\|\|h\|^2, \qquad \|T^*T\|\le\|T^*\|\|T\|=\|T\|^2.∥Th∥2=⟨h,T∗Th⟩≤∥T∗T∥∥h∥2,∥T∗T∥≤∥T∗∥∥T∥=∥T∥2.

Taking the supremum over vectors of norm at most one proves

 ∥T∗T∥=∥T∥2=∥TT∗∥ .\boxed{\ \|T^*T\|=\|T\|^2=\|TT^*\|\ }. ∥T∗T∥=∥T∥2=∥TT∗∥ ​.

This also works between different Hilbert spaces. For completeness of B(H)B(H)B(H), an operator-norm Cauchy sequence (Tn)(T_n)(Tn​) has a pointwise limit Th=lim⁡nTnhTh=\lim_nT_nhTh=limn​Tn​h. The uniform bound on ∥Tn∥\|T_n\|∥Tn​∥ makes TTT bounded and linear. Thus B(H)B(H)B(H), with this adjoint and norm, has exactly the concrete C*-algebra properties used later. The identity has norm one when H≠{0}H\ne\{0\}H={0}.

10.3. The Hilbert tensor product and elementary-vector totality

Start with the free complex vector space on formal symbols (h,k)∈H×K(h,k)\in H\times K(h,k)∈H×K, and quotient by the relations making (h,k)↦h⊗k(h,k)\mapsto h\otimes k(h,k)↦h⊗k bilinear. This is the algebraic tensor space H⊙KH\odot KH⊙K; every element is a finite sum of elementary tensors. Put

⟨∑ihi⊗ki,∑jhj′⊗kj′⟩=∑i,j⟨hi,hj′⟩⟨ki,kj′⟩.\left\langle\sum_i h_i\otimes k_i, \sum_j h'_j\otimes k'_j\right\rangle =\sum_{i,j}\langle h_i,h'_j\rangle\langle k_i,k'_j\rangle.⟨i∑​hi​⊗ki​,j∑​hj′​⊗kj′​⟩=i,j∑​⟨hi​,hj′​⟩⟨ki​,kj′​⟩.

Each bilinearity relation in either tensor variable is respected by the displayed form, conjugate linearly in its first full argument and linearly in its second. The form is therefore well defined on the quotient and conjugate symmetric.

To check positive definiteness, take v=∑ihi⊗kiv=\sum_i h_i\otimes k_iv=∑i​hi​⊗ki​. A finite Gram-Schmidt procedure on the span of its finitely many hih_ihi​ produces an orthonormal basis e1,…,eme_1,\ldots,e_me1​,…,em​: successively subtract the components along the vectors already obtained, discard zero residuals, and divide each remaining residual by its norm. Thus

v=∑r=1mer⊗ℓr,ℓr=∑i⟨er,hi⟩ki,⟨v,v⟩=∑r=1m∥ℓr∥2.v=\sum_{r=1}^m e_r\otimes\ell_r, \qquad \ell_r=\sum_i\langle e_r,h_i\rangle k_i, \qquad \langle v,v\rangle=\sum_{r=1}^m\|\ell_r\|^2.v=r=1∑m​er​⊗ℓr​,ℓr​=i∑​⟨er​,hi​⟩ki​,⟨v,v⟩=r=1∑m​∥ℓr​∥2.

The coefficient ℓr\ell_rℓr​ can also be recovered by the linear map induced by (h,k)↦⟨er,h⟩k(h,k)\mapsto\langle e_r,h\rangle k(h,k)↦⟨er​,h⟩k, so this description respects all tensor relations. If the last sum is zero, every ℓr\ell_rℓr​ is zero and v=0v=0v=0 in the algebraic tensor space. The form is an inner product.

Complete this normed space by Cauchy sequences: identify two Cauchy sequences when their difference tends to zero, and define their inner product as the limit of the termwise inner products. Cauchy-Schwarz makes that limit well defined and independent of representatives. Constant sequences embed H⊙KH\odot KH⊙K isometrically. Every Cauchy-sequence class is a limit of its constant-sequence terms, so their image is dense.

This completion is complete. Indeed, for a Cauchy sequence (xj)(x_j)(xj​) of classes, choose vj∈H⊙Kv_j\in H\odot Kvj​∈H⊙K with ∥vj−xj∥<2−j\|v_j-x_j\|<2^{-j}∥vj​−xj​∥<2−j. The triangle inequality makes (vj)(v_j)(vj​) Cauchy; its class is the limit of (xj)(x_j)(xj​). Denote the resulting Hilbert space by H⊗KH\otimes KH⊗K. Finite sums of elementary tensors are total by this construction, and

∥h⊗k∥=∥h∥∥k∥.\|h\otimes k\|=\|h\|\|k\|.∥h⊗k∥=∥h∥∥k∥.

10.9. Scope of the finite-leg argument

Sections 10.1–10.8 prove the Hilbert tensor completion and totality, mixed compression bounds, restricted vector-functional normality, the unital bicommutant identity, the operator C*-identity, and the factor-center and onto-automorphism calculations used in Lemma 7.1. They use the stated scalar, Hilbert and concrete operator-algebra definitions. Abstract predual equivalence, normal realization, general tensor commutation, trace and modular theorems require the prerequisites stated for their respective results.

11. Modular action of the faithful identical two-level product

This supplies the faithful countable identical two-level instance of Theorem 6.1 used by Constant CAR states and the periodic core, formula (3) and Theorem 3.2. The general statement and original proof of Theorem 6.1 are retained. The hypotheses are invertible ρ=diag⁡(1−p,p)\rho=\operatorname{diag}(1-p,p)ρ=diag(1−p,p), 0<p<10<p<10<p<1, and countably many identical matrix legs.

The foundation boundary is ZFC, real and complex scalar completeness, elementary finite matrix algebra, Hilbert-space and densely defined operator definitions, and the complete concrete proofs in Sections 10.1–10.6. These supply Cauchy–Schwarz, projections, Hilbert Riesz and bounded adjoints, tensor completion/operators, the unital bicommutant theorem, countable Hilbert sums and concrete ultraweak topology. Every further diagonal, domain, graph and expectation argument is supplied below. An abstract predual or existence theorem for a faithful normal representation is not an input.

Inner products are conjugate linear in the first variable and linear in the second. Here normality means continuity for the concrete ultraweak topology of Section 10.6. A graph core means a subspace whose graph is dense in the full graph in the product Hilbert norm.

11.1. Scalar powers and the local Hilbert–Schmidt model

For λ>0\lambda>0λ>0 and real s,ts,ts,t, use

λs=exp⁡(slog⁡λ),λit=exp⁡(itlog⁡λ),\lambda^s=\exp(s\log\lambda),\qquad \lambda^{it}=\exp(it\log\lambda),λs=exp(slogλ),λit=exp(itlogλ),

as constructed in Exponential, logarithm and scalar powers. That proof establishes uniform absolute convergence of the complex exponential series on bounded discs, its addition and conjugation laws and its derivative. The real exponential is a continuous strictly increasing bijection onto (0,∞)(0,\infty)(0,∞), with continuous inverse log⁡\loglog. It proves, in particular,

λs>0,λs+u=λsλu,(λs)u=λsu,∣λit∣=1,λi(t+u)=λitλiu,(λ−1)it=λ−it.\lambda^s>0,\quad \lambda^{s+u}=\lambda^s\lambda^u, \quad (\lambda^s)^u=\lambda^{su},\quad |\lambda^{it}|=1,\quad \lambda^{i(t+u)}=\lambda^{it}\lambda^{iu},\quad (\lambda^{-1})^{it}=\lambda^{-it}.λs>0,λs+u=λsλu,(λs)u=λsu,∣λit∣=1,λi(t+u)=λitλiu,(λ−1)it=λ−it.

The imaginary powers are continuous in ttt, and the positive half power is the unique positive scalar square root. These scalar facts justify the eigenvalue powers below.

11.10. Scope of the matrix calculation

The finite-support eigenbasis determines the closed diagonal operator and half power with their full weighted square-sum domains. The conjugation gives the closed antilinear operator and finite-support graph core. The finite-leg expectations approximate both coordinates of each initial Tomita graph point. These steps identify the full closure and give formulas (MM14)–(MM15) for countably many identical matrix legs with invertible ρ=diag⁡(1−p,p)\rho=\operatorname{diag}(1-p,p)ρ=diag(1−p,p), 0<p<10<p<10<p<1, in the pointed Hilbert–Schmidt completion. Section 11.9 gives the conjugation/commutant identity in this setting.

The general Theorem 6.1 still requires its stated spectral, Tomita and normality prerequisites. The matrix calculation supplies no general type-III invariant, semifiniteness criterion, weight perturbation, KMS uniqueness or modular-centralizer theorem. In particular it does not identify MσM^\sigmaMσ with the trace-commutation centralizer {x:ϕ(xy)=ϕ(yx) for every y∈M}\{x:\phi(xy)=\phi(yx)\text{ for every }y\in M\}{x:ϕ(xy)=ϕ(yx) for every y∈M} for an arbitrary normal state.

12. The type-II1 conclusion for arbitrary trace products

Corollary 5.3 proves the type-II1 conclusion: orthogonal occupation choices in arbitrarily large finite sets prove infinite dimension; the arbitrary-factor matrix-unit theorem shows that a minimal projection, in the presence of the given faithful normalized trace, would force finite dimension. Every step is made for the original arbitrary index set and arbitrary nontrivial finite-factor legs. The exact projection and matrix-unit proof is Constant CAR states, Sections 8.1–8.9. The conclusion uses the factor-type definition, with no general type-decomposition theorem and no separability inference.

13. Elementary calculus

Elementary calculus for infinite products proves scalar completeness and roots, compactness, complex polynomial approximation, the exponential and logarithm, continuous Banach-valued integration, rectangle cancellation, the spectrum, polynomial spectral mapping and the spectral-radius formula. Its setting is ZFC, the ordered complete real field, finite arithmetic and the definitions of the stated normed objects.

14. Scalar and directed interface consequences

The following arguments give the scalar and directed estimates used in the C*-construction.

FI01. Scalar square-root continuity and the cutoff functions

The kernel is not closed because it approximates the exponential, which is not eventually zero. These cutoffs prove the density assertion used in Exercise 11. Finally, for any compatible *-homomorphisms ψn\psi_nψn​ into a C*-algebra, automatic contractivity gives

Every map in the family is zero. In particular every *-representation of the algebraic limit on a Hilbert space is zero, since restricting it to the stages gives such a compatible family.

15. C*-norms, quotients and arbitrary directed limits

F01–F10 prove the norm, functional-calculus, order, ideal and quotient facts needed in Section 1. The scalar and contour arguments are in Elementary calculus for infinite products. F11–F12 give the arbitrary directed limit and its kernels; F14 treats general normed systems. F13 gives an optional faithful isometric nondegenerate representation, including the zero case. It provides no von Neumann topology, tensor norm, bidual or modular theorem.

F15. The limited AF consequence of the selected provider

For a sequence of finite-dimensional C*-algebras, the stage images in the completed limit are finite-dimensional *-subalgebras, are closed, and form an increasing dense union by F11. A finite-dimensional subspace of a normed space is closed: choosing a basis, its unit sphere in the coordinate Euclidean norm is compact, and the continuous norm has a positive minimum on that sphere; therefore coordinate Cauchy sequences converge whenever their linear combinations converge. Conversely, a C*-algebra that is the closure of an increasing sequence of finite-dimensional *-subalgebras is the limit of their inclusion system by F11's universal extension argument. Each finite-dimensional complex stage has a countable dense set of rational real and imaginary coordinates, so the union of those sets is countable and dense; the limit is separable. This is the sequential AF equivalence and its separability consequence. It does not say that an arbitrary directed union of finite-dimensional algebras is separable, nor that every AF or UHF classification theorem has been established.

Its half-power and imaginary powers are the direct sums of DG1/2D_G^{1/2}DG1/2​ and DGitD_G^{it}DGit​: the same domain test and the separate spectral calculus prove these assertions. The displayed finite spectral identity gives Dit=UtD^{it}=U_tDit=Ut​, the coordinatewise modular unitary in Section 6, first on finite-coordinate vectors and then everywhere by its bound one.

The pointed finite-head projection PFP_FPF​ retains exactly the summands G⊂FG\subset FG⊂F. For every η∈Dom⁡D1/2\eta\in\operatorname{Dom}D^{1/2}η∈DomD1/2, finite truncation of the two square sums gives

PFη→η,D1/2PFη→D1/2η.P_F\eta\to\eta,\qquad D^{1/2}P_F\eta\to D^{1/2}\eta.PF​η→η,D1/2PF​η→D1/2η.

The finite tensor graph core already proved above then makes the local MFΩM_F\OmegaMF​Ω vectors a core for the whole product graph. Finally Theorem 4.1 gives EF(x)Ω→xΩE_F(x)\Omega\to x\OmegaEF​(x)Ω→xΩ and EF(x)∗Ω→x∗ΩE_F(x)^*\Omega\to x^*\OmegaEF​(x)∗Ω→x∗Ω for every x∈Mx\in Mx∈M. Thus local algebra vectors approximate both coordinates of every initial Tomita graph point; closing gives exactly S=JD1/2S=JD^{1/2}S=JD1/2, the full graph asserted in Theorem 6.1. This supplies a direct positive-operator construction at arbitrary index and Hilbert-space cardinality, with no restriction to the identical two-level calculation of Section 11.

References and continuation

J. von Neumann, On infinite direct products, Compositio Mathematica 6 (1939), 1–77, Definition 4.1.1, Lemmas 4.1.2–4.1.4 and Theorem V, pp.35–38, develops the pointed finite-support basis. Theorem X, pp.62–63, treats full operator-algebra legs.

Huzihiro Araki and E. J. Woods, A Classification of Factors, Section 2, pp.55–60, develops countable ITPFI reference-vector comparisons. The norm-sum equivalence printed in (2.6), p.55, is false: unit vectors separated by angle 1/n1/n1/n have summable overlap defects but nonsummable norm differences. Section 3 here keeps the conditional-phase requirement for ordered partial tensors. The scanned header gives volume 3 (1968); the publisher catalogue gives volume 4 (1968).

Yoshiomi Nakagami, Infinite Tensor Products of Operators, Publ. RIMS 10 (1974), 111–145, Lemma 4.2, Corollary 4.1 and Lemma 6.1, studies product modular operators. The note on p.145 removes component separability by reference to another paper.

Moritz Weber, Xin Li and Christian Voigt, C*-algebras and dynamics, ISem24 lecture notes, February 20, 2021, Sections 2, 3 and 8.1, develops C*-norms, ideals, quotients and sequential inductive limits. Matthew Daws, Inductive limits of Banach algebras, Sections 2–3, treats arbitrary directed normed systems and compatible-map norm control.

Jesse Peterson, Notes on operator algebras, April 27, 2020, Sections 3.4–3.5 and 6.3, develops concrete operator topologies, the unital bicommutant theorem and the bidual method. Jacob Shapiro, Functional Analysis, MAT520 lecture notes, Theorems 7.6–7.7, 7.10, 7.13 and Claim 7.14, treats the Hilbert-space estimates and adjoints. Connes, Periodic automorphisms of the hyperfinite factor of type II1, Lemma 3.4, p.50, gives a finite-matrix coefficient method.

The CAR applications are developed in Fermions, Fock and quasi-free factors and Constant CAR states and the periodic core.
